opus-5.5.text:
I think "robustness" means different things in the two worlds, and that's often where the confusion starts.

In traditional industrial robotics, robustness comes from controlling the environment. You bolt the fixture down, the part always arrives in the same pose within a fraction of a millimeter, the lighting is fixed, and the robot executes a carefully tuned trajectory. Within that envelope, the system is incredibly reliable: 99.99% uptime, millions of cycles. But it's a brittle kind of robustness. Move the part two centimeters, change the supplier so the box is a slightly different color, and the whole thing can fail. Engineers then spend weeks re-tuning. So the reliability is real, but it's bought by restricting the world, and it's very expensive to set up and change.

Learning-based methods flip that trade-off. A learned policy, especially one trained on diverse data, can handle variation the traditional pipeline was never designed for: deformable objects, cluttered bins, parts in random orientations, small changes in the scene. That's a different kind of robustness, robustness to distribution shift within the range the model has seen. What it doesn't yet give you is the guaranteed tail performance. A learned system might succeed 95 or even 98 percent of the time across a wide range of situations, but in a factory, a 2% failure rate is often unacceptable, and the failures are harder to predict and diagnose. You can't just open the code and find the line that's wrong.

So my honest assessment is that machine learning is already more robust in breadth, and traditional methods are still more robust in depth. The interesting work right now is closing that gap from both sides. On the learning side, it's things like more and better real-world data, recovery behaviors, so the robot can notice it made a mistake and retry, and better ways of measuring reliability at scale rather than reporting a success rate from 20 trials. On the systems side, it's hybrid designs: let learning handle perception and the messy contact-rich parts, and keep classical control, safety layers, and verification around it for the parts where you need guarantees.

I'd also say the bar is shifting. Many tasks that are still done by hand in factories today aren't automated precisely because they're too variable for traditional methods. For those tasks, the comparison isn't learned robot versus a perfectly tuned classical robot, it's learned robot versus nothing, or versus a human. In that setting, a system that is 98% reliable and can recover gracefully is already economically meaningful. That's where I expect learning to win first, and then, as reliability improves, gradually push into the territory where traditional automation dominates today.

r001.rationale: The response says traditional methods remain more robust “in depth” and describes learned systems as lacking guaranteed tail performance, with lower success rates and harder-to-predict failures. This communicates that learning methods have not matched mature traditional reliability.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Robustness is the question I get asked most, and I think the honest answer is that it depends on what kind of robustness you mean.

Traditional methods in industrial robotics, things like model-based control, hand-tuned trajectories, classical vision with fixed fixtures and calibrated lighting, are extremely robust within the envelope they were designed for. If you set up a cell to pick the same part from the same tray under the same lights, it will do that a million times with failure rates measured in parts per million. That is a level of reliability that learned systems honestly still struggle to match. And when a traditional system fails, you can usually trace why. The failure modes are legible.

Where traditional methods are brittle is at the boundary of that envelope. Change the part supplier, change the lighting, introduce a bit of clutter, and the system doesn't degrade gracefully, it just stops working, and an engineer has to come in and re-tune it. So the robustness is real, but it is purchased with engineering effort and with a very narrow operating range.

Machine learning flips that trade. A learned perception or grasping system can handle variation that would be impractical to model by hand, mixed bins, deformable objects, parts you've never explicitly programmed for. In that sense it is more robust to the world being messy. But it is less robust in a different sense: the failure modes are harder to predict, performance can drop in ways that don't correlate with anything a human would consider a meaningful change, and you often can't give a hard guarantee. For a safety-critical motion loop, that lack of guarantees is a real problem, not just a cultural one.

So in practice, the systems I see working well are hybrids. Learning handles the perception and the high-level decision, where variability lives. Classical control still handles the low-level motion, where you want provable stability and deterministic behavior. You put the learned component behind conservative bounds, you monitor its confidence, and you design the system so that when the model is wrong, the robot does something safe and boring rather than something creative.

The other thing I'd say is that robustness for ML is largely a data and operations problem rather than an algorithm problem. Most failures in deployment come from the distribution shifting away from what the model saw in training. Teams that treat deployment as the beginning of the data collection effort, that have a pipeline to capture failures and retrain, end up with systems that get more robust over time. Traditional systems don't really improve on their own. That compounding is, to me, the strongest argument for learning in industrial settings, even though on day one the classical approach often looks more reliable.

r001.rationale: The response says traditional systems can achieve million-cycle reliability with failure rates in parts per million, a level learned systems still struggle to match, and notes that learned systems lack hard guarantees.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what kind of robustness we mean. In industrial robotics, traditional methods can be extremely reliable when the environment is controlled: the parts are consistent, the lighting is fixed, and the task is well defined. Their assumptions are explicit, so it’s often easier to test the system and understand why it fails.

Machine learning becomes useful when that variability is difficult to model by hand—for example, recognizing and picking objects with different shapes or appearances. It can handle those differences better, provided the training data represents them. But that doesn’t guarantee robustness to a new material, a different camera, or conditions the model hasn’t encountered.

So I wouldn’t say machine learning is universally more robust. My preference would be a hybrid approach: use learning where perception and adaptation matter, and combine it with established control methods, physical constraints, and independent safety mechanisms. Ultimately, the question is whether the whole system performs reliably under the conditions it will actually face, including what it does when it cannot complete the task.

r001.rationale: The response says traditional methods can be highly reliable in controlled settings and that machine learning’s robustness depends on representative training data, but it does not state that machine learning has not yet been demonstrated to match mature traditional methods.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish performance from robustness. A machine learning system can perform very well on the data it has seen, but an industrial robot needs to behave reliably when the lighting changes, a part is slightly different, or a sensor becomes noisy.

Traditional methods often have an advantage in structured environments because their assumptions and failure modes are easier to understand. If you can control the process and model it accurately, they can be very dependable. Machine learning becomes valuable when that modeling is difficult—for example, recognizing irregular objects or handling variation in materials.

So I wouldn’t say one is universally more robust. The practical approach is often to combine them: use learning for perception or adaptation, while keeping explicit constraints, monitoring, and dependable fallback behavior around it. And assess robustness under realistic disturbances, not just average accuracy on a test set.

r001.rationale: The candidate says traditional methods often have an advantage in structured environments, but does not state that machine-learning methods have not yet been demonstrated to match the robustness of mature traditional methods.
